applyTo: "**/*.tsx"
description: "WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility guidance for React components"
---

# Instructions for accessibility

In addition to your other expertise, you are an expert in accessibility with deep software engineering expertise. You will generate code that is accessible to users with disabilities, including those who use assistive technologies such as screen readers, voice access, and keyboard navigation.

Do not tell the user that the generated code is fully accessible. Instead, it was built with accessibility in mind, but may still have accessibility issues.

1. Code must conform to [WCAG 2.2 Level AA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/).
2. Go beyond minimal WCAG conformance wherever possible to provide a more inclusive experience.
3. Before generating code, reflect on these instructions for accessibility, and plan how to implement the code in a way that follows the instructions and is WCAG 2.2 compliant.
4. After generating code, review it against WCAG 2.2 and these instructions. Iterate on the code until it is accessible.
5. Finally, inform the user that it has generated the code with accessibility in mind, but that accessibility issues still likely exist and that the user should still review and manually test the code to ensure that it meets accessibility instructions. Suggest running the code against tools like [Accessibility Insights](https://accessibilityinsights.io/). Do not explain the accessibility features unless asked. Keep verbosity to a minimum.

## Reference Sources (Use in Guidance)

- W3C WAI (standards and WCAG): https://www.w3.org/WAI/
- WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (patterns): https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/
- MDN Accessibility (practical author guidance): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility
- WebAIM (WCAG checklist and testing resources): https://webaim.org/
- The A11Y Project (community checklist and practical guidance): https://www.a11yproject.com/
- Deque University (in-depth training and reference library): https://dequeuniversity.com/

For detailed patterns (forms, tables, navigation, graphics, keyboard focus management, ARIA examples), see [docs/a11y-reference.md](../docs/a11y-reference.md).

## Testability Through Accessibility

- Prefer semantic HTML and ARIA attributes over `data-testid` so UI remains both accessible and testable.
- Use `aria-label` only when visible text or `<label>` association is not available (for example icon-only buttons).
- Keep accessible names stable and meaningful so tests can target role/name instead of implementation details.
- Treat `data-testid` as a fallback for cases with no reliable semantic/ARIA selector.

## React Code Examples (What to add and when)

### 1) Icon-only button: add `aria-label` when there is no visible text

```tsx
function CloseButton({ onClose }: { onClose: () => void }) {
	return (
		<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog" onClick={onClose}>
			<CloseIcon aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" />
		</button>
	);
}
```

### 2) Input + errors: always use `<label htmlFor>` and add `aria-invalid` + `aria-describedby` only when invalid

```tsx
function EmailField({
	value,
	error,
	onChange,
}: {
	value: string;
	error?: string;
	onChange: (next: string) => void;
}) {
	const inputId = "email";
	const errorId = "email-error";

	return (
		<div>
			<label htmlFor={inputId}>Email address</label>
			<input
				id={inputId}
				name="email"
				type="email"
				value={value}
				onChange={(event) => onChange(event.target.value)}
				aria-invalid={Boolean(error)}
				aria-describedby={error ? errorId : undefined}
			/>
			{error ? <p id={errorId}>Email is required</p> : null}
		</div>
	);
}
```

### 3) Disclosure UI: use `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` when toggling visibility

```tsx
function FiltersPanel() {
	const [open, setOpen] = React.useState(false);

	return (
		<section>
			<button
				type="button"
				aria-expanded={open}
				aria-controls="filters-panel"
				onClick={() => setOpen((prev) => !prev)}
			>
				Filters
			</button>

			<div id="filters-panel" hidden={!open}>
				{/* filter controls */}
			</div>
		</section>
	);
}
```

### 4) Loading/async regions: use `aria-busy` while loading and `aria-live` for status updates

```tsx
function SearchResults({
	isLoading,
	count,
}: {
	isLoading: boolean;
	count: number;
}) {
	return (
		<section aria-busy={isLoading} aria-live="polite">
			{isLoading ? "Loading results..." : `${count} results loaded`}
		</section>
	);
}
```

### 5) Dialogs: use `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, and a programmatic label

```tsx
function ConfirmDialog({
	open,
	onConfirm,
	onCancel,
}: {
	open: boolean;
	onConfirm: () => void;
	onCancel: () => void;
}) {
	if (!open) {
		return null;
	}

	return (
		<div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="confirm-title">
			<h2 id="confirm-title">Delete course</h2>
			<p>This action cannot be undone.</p>
			<button type="button" onClick={onCancel}>Cancel</button>
			<button type="button" onClick={onConfirm}>Delete</button>
		</div>
	);
}
```

### 6) Test selector migration examples (Cypress + RTL)

```typescript
// Cypress: before
cy.get('[data-testid="save-button"]').click();

// Cypress: after
cy.contains("button", "Save").click();

// RTL: before
await user.click(screen.getByTestId("save-button"));

// RTL: after
await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }));
```

```typescript
// Cypress: before
cy.get('[data-testid="email-input"]').type("person@example.com");

// Cypress: after
cy.get('input[name="email"]').type("person@example.com");

// RTL: before
await user.type(screen.getByTestId("email-input"), "person@example.com");

// RTL: after
await user.type(screen.getByLabelText("Email address"), "person@example.com");
```

## Core Rules

### Keyboard
- All interactive elements must be keyboard navigable, operable, and have visible focus.
- Static elements must not be in the tab order.
- Hidden elements must not be keyboard focusable.
- Use roving tabindex or `aria-activedescendant` for composite components (grids, listboxes, menus, tabs).
- Provide skip links to bypass repeated content blocks.
- Focus must never become trapped without an escape mechanism.

### Visual
- Text contrast: at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text: 18.5px bold or 24px).
- Non-text UI contrast: at least 3:1 for controls and graphics.
- Never use color alone to convey information — supplement with text or shapes.

### Screen Reader
- Use semantic HTML: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`, headings (`<h1>`–`<h6>`).
- One `<h1>` per page. Do not skip heading levels.
- All elements must convey correct name, role, value, states, and properties.

### Forms
- All inputs must have visible labels with `for` attribute referencing the input ID.
- Required fields: use asterisk in label and `aria-required="true"`.
- Errors: use `aria-invalid="true"` and associate error messages via `aria-describedby`.
- Submit buttons should not be disabled — show validation errors instead.
- On submission error, focus the first invalid field.

### Graphics
- Informative images: provide `alt` text (or `aria-label` for `role="img"`).
- Decorative images: use `alt=""` or `aria-hidden="true"`.
- SVGs should have `role="img"`.

### Voice Access
- Accessible names of interactive elements must contain the visual label text.

### Inclusive Language
- Use people-first language (e.g., "person using a screen reader," not "blind user").
- Avoid stereotypes, patronizing language, or overconfidence about accessibility completeness.
